title: Reformed grant grave conscience-wasting sins vs lighter faults compatible with peace and seeing God
source_text: LX. Praeterea docuimus Reformatos agnoscere quaedam esse peccata gravia & atrocia, quae conscientiam vastant: ita ut, quamdiu homo in iis perseverat, actuque & reipsa ab iis non recedit, non possit pro pio & sancto haberi, & in eo statu bonam servare conscientiam, & laetitiam spiritus, ac fiduciam salutis retinere: Alia vero esse peccata leviora, quae non obstant quominus fidelis etiamsi in ea quotidie incurrat, bo-nam conscientiam servet, & eam justitiae ac sanctitatis mensuram retineat, quae in hac vita necessaria est, ut aliquis in futura Deum videre possit; adeoque quae non tol-lunt ex homine pacem internam, & legitimam salutis atque remissionis peccatorum fiduciam.
pass_a_gloss: Besides we have taught that the Reformed acknowledge certain sins to be grave and atrocious which waste the conscience: so that as long as a man perseveres in them and does not actually and in reality withdraw from them, he cannot be held for pious and holy, and in that state keep a good conscience and retain gladness of spirit and confidence of salvation: But that other sins are lighter, which do not hinder the faithful person, even if he runs into them daily, from keeping a good conscience and retaining that measure of righteousness and holiness which in this life is necessary that someone may see God in the future; and so which do not take from a man inward peace and legitimate confidence of salvation and of the remission of sins.
pass_b_english: Reformed mark conscience-wasting graves that bar piety, peace, and salvation-confidence while they last.
Lighter daily faults leave good conscience, the holiness-measure needed to see God, and lawful pardon-trust.

choices.why: Daily lighter recurrence ≠ loss of peace.
